1.sense: Tabaraka is a verb, not an epithet: abundance that settles and stays rather than a quality being praised. The dominion is said to be in his hand, which in Arabic is possession together with control and not a place where a thing is kept. The surah takes its name from that word, mulk, and its first move is to fix the owner before anything owned is described.

notes.t: Tabaraka is form six of b-r-k, the root behind barakah. The related noun birkah is a pool, water that stays instead of running off. The verb is used in the Qur'an only of Allah, in nine places, and never of anything made.

The Prophet ﷺ is told elsewhere to address Allah as the owner of all dominion, who gives it and takes it away, and that verse closes on the same two clauses as this one: good is in your hand, and you are able over every thing.

A report has the Prophet ﷺ say that a surah of thirty verses interceded for a man until he was forgiven, and names it as Tabaraka alladhi biyadihi al-mulk. It is carried by Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah from Abu Hurayra and its grading is discussed.
notes.src: Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah, from Abu Hurayra; graded hasan by Tirmidhi and questioned by others

links.why: the same opening verb, with the dominion spelled out as the heavens and the earth and what is between them
tabaraka opening a surah again, there over the sending down of the criterion

2.sense: Death is named first, and both death and life are objects of the verb created, so neither is a bare absence. Bala is to test by putting under strain, the way a metal is assayed, and what the test is looking for is named exactly: not the most deeds but the best. The two names at the close hold the test between them, one who cannot be overcome and one who covers over.

notes.t: The clause to test which of you is best in deed is fixed wording. Hud ends its creation account with it, and Al-Kahf uses it of the ornament put on the earth, so the test is attached to the world as made rather than to one occasion.
The comparative is ahsan, best, not akthar, most. Quantity is not the thing being weighed, and the verse says so before any deed is described.
Al-Aziz and al-Ghafur are an odd pair to end a verse about testing. One name says the outcome cannot be forced, the other that it can be waived.

links.why: every soul tasting death, with the testing named as evil and good together
the human being made from a mingled drop in order to be tested, and given hearing and sight for it

3.sense: Tibaq is layering, one thing set flush over another like the plies of a binding. Tafawut is disparity, the gap between parts that were meant to meet, and its denial is not a claim that the creation is uniform but that nothing in it is out of true. The sentence then stops describing and hands over an instruction and a question: look again, and report a flaw if one is there.

notes.t: Tafawut is from f-w-t, to slip past or miss. The picture is a seam that does not line up, two pieces made to a different measure. What is denied is mismatch, not variety.
Futur is from f-t-r, a splitting along a line, the root behind fitrah and iftar. The flaw the eye is sent to find is named with the same word the Qur'an uses for what the sky finally does.
Seven heavens in layers appear again in Nuh, put there as an argument from something the audience could already be asked to look at.

links.why: the sky built above them with no gaps in it, the same inspection with a different noun
the sky splitting along its seam, the flaw arriving as an event

4.sense: The order is repeated and raised, and karratayni in Arabic idiom is not strictly two but again and again. What comes back is the gaze itself, and it comes back with two words attached to it. Khasi' is used of a dog driven off with a shout, and hasir of a mount ridden until it can go no further, so the search wears out the searcher and leaves the thing searched untouched.

notes.t: Khasa'a is the verb for driving a dog away. The gaze returns not merely empty but rebuffed, sent back by what it went to inspect.
Hasir is from h-s-r, to strip bare, and is used of a camel ridden past its strength. Between the two words the eye is both repelled and spent.
Sight is said elsewhere not to reach him while he reaches sight. The failure here is a failure at the work, not a defect in the work.

links.why: the same command to look, aimed at the camel, the sky, the mountains and the earth in turn
the eye sent out a second time later in the surah, to the birds holding above

5.sense: Misbah is a lamp with a wick, a household object, and the sky nearest to the earth is fitted out with them. The same lights carry two jobs, ornament for what is under them and something thrown at what tries to climb through. Ad-dunya is the feminine of adna, nearest, so the sky being described is the one people can see.

notes.t: Ad-dunya is from d-n-w, to be near. The word the Qur'an uses for this world is the same word: the near one, named by its distance from what follows it.
As-Saffat sets the two functions side by side in one breath, the lowest sky adorned with the planets and guarded against every rebellious devil.
Rujum is from rajama, to throw stones. As-sa'ir, the blaze, closes the verse and comes back twice in the next six as the name of the people who belong to it.

links.why: the jinn's own account of finding the sky filled with stern guards and flames
the one who steals a hearing pursued by a clear flame

6.sense: The punishment prepared for the devils in the verse before is extended, in the next sentence, to human beings, and the two are put in one fire without a break between the verses. Masir is from sara, to become or to end up as, so the word is not only where a road stops but what the traveller has turned into by then. Bi'sa is the fixed verb of blame in Arabic, the exact counterpart of ni'ma.

notes.t: Masir is a noun of place built from sara, to come to be. It names an outcome and a destination with one word.
Wretched is the destination is a set closing formula in the Qur'an, attached to the fire in a run of places, so a reader meets it as a refrain and not as a fresh statement.
The turn from devils to people happens without a joint. The surah does not treat the two as separate cases with separate ends.

links.why: the wrongdoers among the jinn described as firewood for the same fire

7.sense: Ulqu is the verb for tossing a thing, not for leading it in. The first thing reported is a sound, and shahiq is breath dragged inward, the second half of a donkey's bray and the noise of someone sobbing. The fire is boiling while it makes it, so the sound belongs to the fire rather than to the people who have just landed in it.

notes.t: Shahiq is the indrawn breath and zafir the pushed out one. Hud gives both to the damned themselves; here the fire has the sound and the roles are turned around.

Tafur is used of a pot at a rolling boil and of a spring forcing water up. The same verb describes the oven that gushed at the start of Nuh's flood, so the picture is of something driven up from below rather than of flame.
The order of the sentence is thrown, then hear. Nothing is seen; the scene is built out of noise.

links.why: the fire heard from a great distance, its rage and its roaring audible before arrival

8.sense: Tamayyaza is to come apart into separate pieces, one mass ceasing to hold together. Ghayz is rage kept in the chest, not the shouted kind, and the fire is nearly torn open by it. Each arrival is met with a single question from the keepers, and the question is about whether notice was given, not about what was done.

notes.t: The root m-y-z is the one behind the command on the last day for the guilty to stand apart from everyone else. Here the fire itself is close to coming apart at its seams.
Az-Zumar stages the same scene with the same keepers asking the same thing, put there as messengers from among yourselves reciting your Lord's signs to you.
The keepers ask about a warner and nothing else. The whole surah turns on whether warning reached people, which is why this is the only question at the gate.

links.why: the keepers named: angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey what they are commanded
the keepers made angels and their number itself made a trial

9.sense: Bala is the particle that answers a negative question by overturning it, so the admission is complete in the first word. What follows is a quotation of themselves: they denied the man and then denied the whole category, that anything had been sent down at all. The sentence ends with the charge they used to make, repeated in the one place where it can no longer be defended.

notes.t: Bala answers a negative question in the affirmative where na'am would agree with the negation. The confession is built into the grammar before any content arrives.
Al-An'am reports the same denial in almost the same words, that Allah has not sent down anything to a human being, and says of it that they did not measure Allah with his true measure.
Great error is thrown at the warners here and the word comes back at the end of the surah, where the reply is that it will be known who is in plain error.

links.why: the same cry from inside the fire, answered by the reminder that a warner had already come
messengers sent one after another and each community denying its own

10.sense: Two faculties are named and both are given up as unused: taking a thing on report and working it out for oneself. Sama' here is not the ear functioning but attention paid to what was said. The sentence is a conditional in the past, the form Arabic uses for a condition that can no longer be met.

notes.t: Listening and reasoning cover the two ways a claim can be received, from someone who knows or by one's own working. The confession is that neither route was taken, not that the case was examined and rejected.

Al-Furqan puts the same two verbs together in a question about whether most of them hear or reason, and answers that they are like cattle. The words the damned use of themselves here are the words used about them there.
Ashab is a stronger word than inmate. It is used of a man's companions and of the people of a town, so the fire is named as something they belong to.

links.why: ears that do not hear and hearts that do not understand, the organs present and idle
the worst of creatures named as the deaf and dumb who do not reason

11.sense: I'tarafa is to acknowledge a thing as known, built on the root of ma'rifah. The confession is made in full and changes nothing, which is why it is placed here and not earlier. Suhqan is a curse of distance, from sahiq, far off, and from sahaqa, to grind a thing to powder.

notes.t: Suhqan is the accusative Arabic uses for a wish flung at someone, like bu'dan, be far. The root carries remoteness and grinding down at once.
The related adjective sahiq is used of the far-off place a wind drops a falling man into, which fixes the distance the curse is asking for.
Sin is singular, dhanb, not the plural. One admission covers the whole file.

links.why: the same verb of confession used from inside, followed by a request for a way out

12.sense: The turn is abrupt, straight from the fire to the people who feared what they never saw. Khashyah is fear with knowledge inside it, the fear of someone who has grasped what he is dealing with, which is not the same as fright. Bil-ghayb attaches either to the one feared or to the one fearing, a Lord who is unseen or a servant unseen by anyone else, and the Arabic does not choose between them.

notes.t: Bil-ghayb is grammatically open. It can qualify the object, fearing him while he is out of sight, or the subject, fearing him where no one is watching. Both readings are carried by the same three words.
Fatir says that it is the knowledgeable among his servants who fear Allah, which is what separates khashyah from ordinary fear: it follows from knowing what is there.

The hadith of the seven whom Allah shades on the day when there is no shade includes a man who remembered Allah alone and whose eyes overflowed. Fear in the unseen is described there as an act with a place in a list of acts.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Abu Hurayra

links.why: the same phrase with the same two rewards, forgiveness and a generous wage
the one who feared the Merciful unseen and arrived with a turning heart

13.sense: A command in form and an argument in effect: whisper it or shout it, the result is identical. Asarra is to drop the voice to a confidant and jahara to raise it so everyone hears, and between them they use up the ways a thing can be said. The answer then goes past speech altogether, to dhat as-sudur, what a chest holds and never let out.

notes.t: Dhat as-sudur is an idiom for the possessions of the chest, what belongs to it rather than what leaves it. The verse exhausts speech in its first half so that the second half can name something further in.
Ta Ha puts the same argument the other way up: if you speak aloud, he knows the secret and what is more hidden still.
The verse sits between the promise to those who fear unseen and the question about whether the maker knows. Concealment is the hinge the passage turns on.

links.why: the one who hides his words and the one who says them openly held to be alike, along with the man moving by night
hiding what is in the chests or showing it, with the same outcome

14.sense: A question with its answer inside it. Man khalaqa reads two ways, as the subject, does the maker not know, or as the object, does he not know what he made, and the grammar leaves both open onto the same reply. The two names then say how the knowing works: latif is fine enough to reach into small places, khabir is knowledge of a thing from the inside.

notes.t: Man khalaqa can be the subject of the verb or its object. Arabic permits both and neither reading changes the answer, which is why the verse does not disambiguate.
Latif is used of what is fine enough to pass through; khabir is from khabara, to know a matter by having gone into it. The pair covers reach and depth.
Luqman ends the image of a mustard seed hidden inside a rock with these same two names, which is where their joint sense is easiest to see.

links.why: sight not grasping him while he grasps sight, closed with the same two names

15.sense: Dhalul is the word for a broken-in camel, one that carries a rider without fighting him, and the earth is described that way before anything is asked of it. Two commands follow from the description, walk and eat. Manakib is the plural of mankib, the shoulder, so the ground stays an animal all the way through the sentence, and the sentence ends by naming where the walking stops.

notes.t: Dhalul is from dh-l-l, lowness, but as an adjective for an animal it means tractable rather than humiliated. A dhalul camel is one that can be ridden.
Nuh makes the same argument with different furniture, the earth spread as a carpet so that people can travel its broad roads.
Manakib is glossed by the commentators as the roads, as the mountains, and as the outlying tracts of the earth. The image of shoulders is agreed on and its application is not.
notes.src: read as roads, as mountains and as outlying regions in the classical commentaries; no one reading is settled

links.why: nushur used of dead land brought back by rain, the same word for the same act
the surah's other closing on the same idea, gathering in place of rising

16.sense: The argument turns to threat, and the first threat is the ground. Khasafa is used of the earth taking a thing down out of sight, and mawr is the churning of what had been still, a swell running through something solid. What is being questioned is the safety people take from the floor under them without ever deciding to.

notes.t: Khasafa is to make a thing sink and vanish. The same verb is used of the moon in eclipse, its light going down out of view rather than being put out.
Al-Qasas uses the verb of Qarun, swallowed along with his house, so the punishment named here already had a case attached to it.
Mawr is a rolling, wavelike motion, used elsewhere of the sky on the last day. The earth is given the movement of something that was built not to move.

links.why: the same two threats in the same order, the land swallowing and a storm of stones
the question put to those who plot, whether they are safe from the earth swallowing them

17.sense: The second question moves the threat from under the feet to overhead. Hasib is a wind carrying gravel, from hasa, pebbles, and it is the word used for what was sent on the people of Lut. The sentence does not finish as a question but breaks into a promise, and nadhir at the end means the warning itself, its possessive ending clipped in the old style.

notes.t: Nadhir here and nakir in the next verse both carry a dropped possessive ya, my warning and my rejection. The shortened form is what lets the two verses rhyme.
Al-Qamar uses hasib of what was sent on the people of Lut, with Lut's family excepted from it, so the word arrives already carrying a case.
The two questions together cover both directions, the ground opening beneath and the sky throwing down. Between them there is no third place to stand.

links.why: the catalogue of punishments, each people taken by a different one and none of them wronged

18.sense: The threat is closed off with a fact rather than a warning. Denial is not new, and the older cases have already been settled and can be checked. Nakir is from n-k-r, to refuse to acknowledge, so their refusal to know him is answered with a noun built from the same root.

notes.t: Nakir is the answering refusal. The root gives munkar, what is disowned, and nakira, to fail to recognise; the verse turns the word back on the people who acted it.
The clause how was my rejection is a fixed close in the Qur'an, used after the denial of earlier peoples in more than one place.
The question is left without an answer here because the answer stood on the trade road: the Meccans are told elsewhere that they pass the ruins in the morning and at night.

links.why: the same question closing the same argument, after the messengers had been denied

19.sense: The eye is sent out a second time in this surah, now at something ordinary and overhead. Saffat is a participle and yaqbidna a finite verb: the spread wing is the bird's standing state, the fold is the act it keeps repeating inside that state. What holds a heavy body up in thin air is then named, and the name chosen is the Merciful.

notes.t: The grammar splits deliberately. A participle for what holds and a verb for what recurs is an exact description of how a bird actually flies.
An-Nahl has the same sentence with Allah in place of the Merciful, and adds that the birds are held subject in the open air of the sky.
The name could have been Allah, as it is in the parallel. Holding a bird up is put under the name of mercy instead, and the surah keeps returning to that name in the verses that follow.

links.why: the sky held back from falling on the earth, the same verb for holding
Allah holding the heavens and the earth from slipping out of place

20.sense: Amman hadha alladhi is a stack of pointing words, the Arabic of a challenge: name him, produce him. Jund is a body of troops, one singular word for a whole force, so the question offers them everything they might muster in a single breath. Ghurur is being taken in by an appearance, from gharra, to deceive with something that looks good.

notes.t: The pile of demonstratives is a challenge to name a name. English would reach for something like: who exactly, then.
Ya Sin turns the same picture over: gods taken up so that their people might be helped, who cannot help, while the worshippers stand as an army mustered for them.
The root of ghurur also gives ghurrah, the white blaze on a horse's forehead, the thing the eye goes to first. What is charged is not a mistake about the facts but being drawn in by a surface.

links.why: the deceiver named outright, with a warning against being deluded about Allah himself
the question put on the day itself, where is what you worshipped, can they help you now

21.sense: The second challenge drops from defence to food. Amsaka is the verb from two verses back, where nothing holds the birds up but the Merciful, and here the same hand closes instead of holding. Lajja is to keep on at a thing after being checked, and the two nouns give the direction of the persistence: utuww is going past a limit, nufur is bolting like a startled animal.

notes.t: Holding up and holding back are one verb in Arabic. The surah uses both faces of amsaka within three verses, once as the thing that keeps birds in the air and once as the thing that could stop the food.
Fatir states the rule the question depends on: what Allah opens of mercy no one can hold back, and what he holds back no one can send on afterwards.
Nufur closes this verse as nushur closed the earlier one about walking the earth and eating from it. The rhyme holds together a rising and a bolting away.

links.why: the crop put to the same test, and the admission that would follow if it were made debris
the same question asked once more at the end of the surah, about water

22.sense: Two walkers, and the picture settles the question before it is asked. Mukibb is stooped forward onto the face, the gait of someone who cannot see ahead and meets the ground before he meets anything else. The second man gets a posture and a road; the first gets a posture and no road at all, and that imbalance is the whole argument.

notes.t: The first walker is given no surface to be walking on. Everything the sentence supplies to the second, direction and a way, is withheld from the first.
Akabba is one of the verbs the grammarians single out: the fourth form here is intransitive, to fall on one's own face, while the plain form kabba means to throw someone else down.
Al-Furqan describes the same people gathered on their faces towards Hell, worse in place and further astray in road, so the walk carries on past death.

links.why: the same posture on the day of rising, blind and dumb and deaf
the straight path named as one road with the others scattering off it

23.sense: Ansha'a is to raise and grow, the verb used of bringing up a plant and of bringing up a child, so the making is a process and not one stroke. Three faculties are then listed, and they are the three the surah has been working on: the ear that would not listen, the eye sent to look twice, and the heart that keeps what is never said aloud. The count at the end is of thanks, not of faculties.

notes.t: Where the Qur'an names them together, sam' stays singular and absar goes plural. Hearing is one undirected act; seeing is many, each of them aimed.
An-Nahl gives the identical list at birth, when a person knows nothing at all, and ends it with the hope of thanks. Here the same list ends with the observation that thanks are rare.
Fu'ad, plural af'idah, is connected by the lexicographers with a root used of roasting, as against qalb, the heart named for turning. The organ of understanding is named by its heat.

links.why: the same three given after the spirit is breathed in, closed with the same clause about thanks
hearing, sight and heart each held answerable for what it did

24.sense: Dhara'a is to sow broadcast, seed thrown so that it lands apart. Hashara is the opposite motion, driving scattered things back into one place, the verb used of herding. One verse holds both halves of a single movement, out and then in, with nothing said about the interval.

notes.t: The two verbs are opposite motions of the same hand, scattering seed and driving a herd together. Nothing between them is described.
Al-Mu'minun carries this pair of sentences in the same order, the hearing and the sights and the hearts with little thanks, then the scattering in the earth and the gathering to him.
Hashr is used of flushing game or troops out of every corner into one field. The passive here leaves no one doing the walking.

links.why: the dead land revived by rain and the same conclusion drawn about the dead

25.sense: The question is not asked for information. Wa'd in Arabic covers a promise and a threat with one word, and what is being demanded is a date for the appointment just described. The verb is plural, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and everyone repeating what he says, so the demand is made of a community.

notes.t: Wa'd is neutral between promise and threat; wa'id is the narrower word for a threat alone. The deniers use the broad word and ask only for a date.
The same sentence is quoted from deniers in the same words across several surahs, which makes it a standing objection rather than one occasion's remark.
The plural you takes in the Prophet ﷺ and whoever carries his message. The reply in the next verse narrows it back to one man with one job.

links.why: the same demand answered by a single blast that catches them mid-argument
those who do not believe in it hurrying it on, those who do afraid of it

26.sense: Two innama clauses, each fencing something off. Knowledge of the time sits with Allah and nowhere else; the office of the Prophet ﷺ is warning and nothing else, and the second limit is the answer to the question the first one refuses. Mubin is both plain in itself and making plain, so the warner is clear and clarifies.

notes.t: Innama restricts. It puts one thing on one side and everything else on the other, and the verse uses it twice: once about where knowledge is, once about what the messenger is for.
Al-A'raf has the Prophet ﷺ asked when the Hour will drop anchor and told to answer that its knowledge is with his Lord.
In the hadith of Jibril the Prophet ﷺ is asked about the Hour and answers that the one asked knows no more about it than the one asking.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Umar ibn al-Khattab

links.why: the Hour listed among what he alone holds, beside the rain and what is in the wombs
the questioner asked what he has to do with naming it at all

27.sense: The tense jumps forward and the demand of two verses back is answered by putting the thing in front of them. Zulfah is nearness, from the root of drawing close, so what they wanted dated is instead brought near. Si'at is passive, from sa'a, to be bad: the faces are acted on, and the sentence attaches the damage to the face rather than to the person behind it.

notes.t: The verb is passive and the subject is faces. Nothing is reported about what the people do, only about what happens to the part of them that cannot be hidden.
Al-Qiyamah divides that day along the same line, faces bright and looking towards their Lord against faces drawn in and expecting a back-breaking blow.

Tadda'un is the eighth form and the commentators divide over it: what you used to call for, that is, ask to be brought on, or what you used to claim was false. The demand quoted two verses earlier fits the first.
notes.src: read both as calling for it and as claiming about it; both readings are current in the commentaries

links.why: the two sets of faces on that day, one lit up and one under dust
the promise arriving suddenly and stunning them, with no power to turn it back

28.sense: The Meccans were waiting for the small community around the Prophet ﷺ to be finished off. The question hands them that outcome and shows that it settles nothing, because either branch leaves the questioner exactly where he stands. Ajara is to extend protection to someone from outside one's own clan, the arrangement Mecca actually ran on, so the challenge is put in the city's own vocabulary.

notes.t: Ajara is the verb of jiwar, protection given by a clan to an outsider. The question is who will stand surety, put to people who knew precisely what that meant.
Al-Jinn has the Prophet ﷺ say that no one can protect him from Allah either, so the question is not claiming an exemption for his own side.
Destruction and mercy are set out as equally open and neither is argued for. The weight of the sentence is entirely in the clause that follows both.

links.why: the one who gives protection while none is given against him, with dominion in his hand as at the surah's opening
the same waiting for fate to remove him, answered with: wait, I am waiting alongside you

29.sense: The answer to the challenges is a name and two verbs in the first person plural, spoken for a community rather than for one man. Tawakkul is from wakala, to hand a matter to an agent to conduct; it is delegation and not resignation. The last clause returns the charge the deniers made earlier in the surah and leaves the question of who it lands on to be settled later.

notes.t: Tawakkala ala is to appoint someone as one's wakil, one's agent in a matter. The word is legal before it is devotional, and it carries the sense of a case handed over to be run by someone else.
Earlier in the surah the deniers tell the warners they are in great error. The same word comes back here with the identity of the one in error left open.
Ar-Rahman is the name this surah keeps returning to: the creation with no flaw in it, the birds held above, the army that does not exist, and now the answer to who.

links.why: the same reliance stated in the middle of a threat, with every creature held by its forelock
the same standoff put as a bare alternative, one of us on guidance or in plain error

30.sense: The surah ends on the smallest thing it has named. Ghawr is water gone down into the ground past the reach of a well, and ma'in is water running where the eye can follow it, so the two words are opposite depths of the same thing. Asbaha is to enter the morning and by extension to come to be, which sets the loss at daybreak, discovered rather than watched.

notes.t: Ma'in is connected by the lexicographers with ayn, which is both an eye and a spring. Water that can be seen and water that sees are one word apart.
Asbaha puts the change at waking. Nothing is described happening; there is only the well that has stopped giving.
Al-Waqi'ah runs the same argument on drinking water, asking who sent it down from the rain cloud and noting that it could as easily have been made bitter.
The surah opens with the dominion of everything in one hand and closes with a mouthful of water. The distance between the two is the argument it has been making throughout.

links.why: a garden's water sunk beyond reach, with the same two words, asbaha and ghawran
rain sent down by measure and settled in the ground, with the power to take it away stated outright
